slides.title: Surfaces In Three Dimensions
slides.notes: Open by stressing the shift from curves to surfaces: one parameter becomes two, and one coordinate picture is no longer enough. The lecture goal is not to memorize examples, but to learn the local tests that make surface calculus independent of the chosen patch.

slides.title: Route Through The Chapter
slides.notes: The chapter has a clean logical spine: define local coordinate pieces, demand smooth regular overlap behavior, then build tangent planes and normals from those pieces. Keep returning to the same question: which data belongs to the surface, and which data belongs only to the chosen coordinates?

slides.title: A Patch Is A Promise
slides.notes: A surface patch is more than a parametrized drawing. It includes an open parameter domain, a one-to-one image on its surface piece, and enough inverse continuity to use the parameters as local coordinates. The cylinder visual is a good place to emphasize that a seam can be a coordinate decision rather than a geometric defect.

slides.title: Atlases Make Surfaces
slides.notes: Use the atlas slide to separate two ideas that students often merge: the surface is the object being covered, while charts are temporary coordinate windows. Overlaps are not an annoyance; they are the mechanism that lets local calculus agree from one window to another.

slides.title: Regularity Is Rank Two
slides.notes: The cross product test says that the two parameter directions must span a genuine plane in space. If the cross product vanishes, the formula may still draw a set, but it does not supply an allowable surface coordinate patch at that point.

slides.title: Reparametrization Preserves The Test
slides.notes: This is the first major invariance calculation of the chapter. A coordinate change multiplies the old normal area vector by the determinant of its Jacobian, so nonzero determinants preserve regularity. The sign of the determinant already foreshadows orientation.

slides.title: Smooth Maps Are Tested In Charts
slides.notes: A map between surfaces is smooth when its coordinate representative is smooth on compatible chart domains. The cylinder wrapping example is useful because it is locally well behaved but globally many-to-one, so smoothness and global injectivity should not be conflated.

slides.title: Local Diffeomorphism Is Not Global Diffeomorphism
slides.notes: Pause on the distinction between local invertibility and global one-to-one behavior. A full turn in the angle coordinate returns to the same point on the cylinder, even though every small angular interval has a smooth inverse chart. This prepares students for later manifold examples where local information is powerful but incomplete.

slides.title: Tangent Planes From Parameter Curves
slides.notes: The tangent plane is built from velocities of curves that lie on the surface. In a patch, the coordinate curves give two distinguished tangent directions, and all other surface curve velocities are their linear combinations by the chain rule.

slides.title: Derivatives Push Tangent Velocities
slides.notes: The derivative of a smooth surface map should be read as a linear map between tangent planes, not merely as a matrix floating between coordinate grids. Coordinates compute it, but the chain rule is what proves the result is independent of the chosen curve and chart description.

slides.title: Standard Unit Normals
slides.notes: Normal vectors come from the ordered pair of parameter directions, so switching chart orientation can reverse the sign. The sphere example is a useful reminder that a standard normal for a patch need not be the outward normal that geometric intuition first expects.

slides.title: Oriented Angle Needs A Normal
slides.notes: The sign of an angle in a tangent plane depends on the chosen unit normal. With the opposite normal, the same ordered pair of tangent vectors receives the opposite signed angle. This is the local algebraic reason orientability matters.

slides.title: Orientability Means Normals Glue
slides.notes: Orientability is not the existence of a normal at each individual point; local normals always exist for a regular patch. The point is whether chart choices can be arranged so transition determinants stay positive and the local normal choices agree globally.

slides.title: The Mobius Band Obstruction
slides.notes: The Mobius band is the chapter's clean obstruction example because every small piece is a regular surface patch, yet one circuit reverses a transported normal. Ask students to inspect the end of the trip: the base point returns, but the normal direction does not.

slides.title: Patch Doctor Checklist
slides.notes: This slide turns the chapter into a diagnostic workflow. Before trusting a parametrization, identify the domain, compute the two partial derivatives, inspect the cross product, and decide whether excluded points are coordinate seams or actual singularities.

slides.title: What Survives A Change Of Patch
slides.notes: Close by naming the invariant objects that the chapter successfully constructs: the surface as an atlas, tangent planes, derivatives, and orientability. The strongest takeaway is that formulas are useful only after their coordinate dependence has been accounted for.
